improvements.mechanism_cubrid: For the non-MCV mass of a string histogram the estimator LIKE-tests one representative value per bucket - the bucket upper boundary bucket_hi - and, once the histogram has >=100 entries, uses that matching-bucket fraction directly as the selectivity. A bucket boundary is an artefact of sort order, so a suffix pattern uncorrelated with that order matches boundaries at a rate unrelated to its true frequency. The resulting selectivity flows into make_pred_from_bitset(), which orders AND-predicates by selectivity and consults its own heavy/light rank ONLY when two selectivities are exactly equal; so p_type like '%BRASS' (est 0.00921158, actual 0.19979) is placed ahead of p_size = 15 (est 0.02, actual 0.0198) and runs on all 2,000,000 part rows.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: histogram_selectivity() applies the operator function across the histogram bound array and mcv_selectivity() across the MCV list, and patternsel combines both, so a leading-wildcard pattern is still estimated from values that actually occur: 0.26099 vs a true 0.19979 (1.31x). PostgreSQL's order_qual_clauses() then orders quals strictly by cost_qual_eval_node() per-tuple cost - though for this query textlike carries the same default procost as int4eq, so PostgreSQL ALSO evaluates the LIKE first; it is simply not hurt by it.

improvements.explanation: CUBRID pays codepoint decoding and collation-weight mapping per character for a predicate where byte equality would be sufficient, making its LIKE 8.64-9.75x more expensive per row than PostgreSQL's.
improvements.implementation_direction: Add an early fast path in lang_strmatch_utf8() (or dispatch from qstr_eval_like()) for deterministic built-in collations where both operands are ASCII: compare bytes directly and advance with an inlined continuation-byte skip, mirroring PostgreSQL's MatchText/NextChar. Secondarily make intl_utf8_to_cp and intl_nextchar_utf8 inlinable (static inline in a header, or hidden visibility) to remove the 2.82% PLT overhead.
improvements.mechanism_cubrid: lang_strmatch_utf8() advances one character at a time and per position calls intl_utf8_to_cp() on both the target and the pattern, then maps each resulting codepoint through the collation weight table before comparing. There is no ASCII fast path and no byte-lockstep comparison, so a pure-ASCII pattern against an ASCII column still pays two codepoint decodes plus two table lookups per character. The profile shows both decode helpers reached through the dynamic linker on every character: intl_utf8_to_cp 4.82% + @plt 1.75%, intl_nextchar_utf8 3.09% + @plt 1.07% - 2.82% of total query CPU is PLT stub overhead alone.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: MatchText() documents and implements byte-by-byte comparison even for multi-byte encodings, on the grounds that text and pattern stay in lockstep outside wildcard handling, and advances characters with a two-instruction inline macro that just skips UTF-8 continuation bytes. No codepoint is materialized, no weight table is consulted, and there is no out-of-line call in the inner loop.

improvements.mechanism_cubrid: Each parallel worker executes a private clone of the sub-plan below the parallel scan. When a worker finishes, merge_xasl_tree() folds its XASL clone into the coordinator's tree. For the nested-loop chain it iterates the scan_ptr list and calls xasl_merge_stats(xptr1, main) for every level. xasl_merge_stats does not merge a single node: its last statement is iterate_xasl_tree(src, merge_stats, true), which recurses through scan_ptr (xasl_iteration.hpp:189-191) and merges every node in the subtree by header.id with +=. So the level-2 node is merged once (from the caller's first iteration), the level-3 node twice (once inside level-2's subtree walk, once from the caller's second iteration), the level-4 node three times, and a level-k node (k-1) times. The output row counts, and therefore query results, are unaffected - only the trace counters are.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: PostgreSQL keeps a per-worker NodeInstrumentation array in DSM and merges it with planstate_tree_walker (execParallel.c:1173), which visits every PlanState exactly once; for the node being visited it loops over the worker slots and calls InstrAggNode once per worker (execParallel.c:1115). The merge primitive itself (instrument.c:232) touches only the node handed to it and never re-walks children, so no node can be visited by two overlapping traversals.

improvements.implementation_direction: Ordered by evidence strength. (1) Per-scan readahead: issue posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_WILLNEED) for the next run of pages of a sequential or index-range scan, reusing the parameter machinery already present for the mount-time advise (file_io.c:3050) - this overlaps the kernel copy with executor work without any new buffer state, and has direct upstream precedent. (2) Batch the miss path: when the requesting scan is sequential, fetch a run of adjacent pages with the existing fileio_read_pages() (file_io.c:4211) in one call - justified by call-overhead reduction only, NOT by submission-count parity, which the measurement refutes. (3) Only if (1) and (2) prove insufficient, scope genuine asynchronous data-page I/O with in-flight buffer states; the measured total-CPU-per-byte comparison says this must be justified by critical-path latency, not by CPU savings.
improvements.measurement:
Matched plan shape (/*+ USE_HASH */ versus PostgreSQL native, identical per-node row counts).
Critical-path kernel I/O cost: CUBRID rep_movs_alternative 5.95% x 50.36 = 3.00 core-seconds inside cub_server's query threads (profile-cubrid-hash-flat.txt); PostgreSQL next_uptodate_folio 2.48% + rep_movs_alternative 1.58% = 4.06% x 19.28 = 0.78 core-seconds inside leader+workers (profile-pg-flat.txt), plus 2.72 core-seconds of pg_io_worker CPU recorded as auxiliary (Q03-postgresql-telemetry-run1.json). Difference on the critical path: 2.22 core-seconds = 7.9% of the 28.04 core-second excess.
Bytes and syscalls per statement (/proc/<pid>/io): CUBRID rchar 13,594,346,680 (12.66 GiB) in syscr 829,884 read calls = 17.2 KiB per call; PostgreSQL rchar 8,694,806,235 (8.10 GiB) in syscr 551,551 = 15.4 KiB per call. Device read_bytes ~0 on both sides (CUBRID 0.00 MiB, PostgreSQL 0.12 MiB), so this is page-cache copy and syscall cost, never disk latency.
Native CUBRID plan for context: 831,427 corrected page misses (IMP-005 correction applied; the corrected count x 16 KiB = 12.69 GiB matches the independently measured rchar of 13.09 GiB per statement to 3.3%, whereas the uncorrected trace count would imply 25.4 GiB, i.e. 1.92x more than the measured syscall bytes - which is what proves the correction), kernel band 18.07% x 21.91 = 3.96 core-seconds, and IPC collapses to 0.94 versus 1.96 at matched shape.
REJECTED sub-hypothesis, with the number that rejected it: 'CUBRID lacks read combining, so it issues far more I/O submissions than PostgreSQL at io_combine_limit=16.' The code fact is real (fileio_read reads exactly one page; fileio_read_pages is log-only), but the measurement refutes any submission-count penalty: CUBRID moves 17.2 KiB per read syscall versus PostgreSQL's 15.4 KiB, and PostgreSQL's 551,551 calls for ~900,213 block reads (746,768 heap + 153,445 temp) average only 1.63 blocks per call, not 16. Read combining is therefore NOT claimed as an effect here.

Q04 (structurally identical plans on both engines, no hint needed):
276,950 blocking pread() calls per statement at 16,377 bytes each - exactly one 16 KiB page per call, confirming the single-page read path - all issued from cub_server 'parallel-query' executor threads, against 415 read syscalls on PostgreSQL (667.3x). rchar 4,535,681,928 B/statement vs 1,390,736 B. The call graph resolves 10.18% of CUBRID's CPU to rep_movs_alternative reached ONLY via __libc_pread64 <- fileio_read <- pgbuf_claim_bcb_for_fix <- pgbuf_fix_release; with filemap_get_read_batch 1.26% and filemap_read 0.69% the band is 12.13% = 1.160 core-s against PostgreSQL's 0.000 core-s.
SCOPE NOTE: on Q04 the io-worker contrast that motivated this candidate on Q03 does NOT apply, because PostgreSQL performs zero physical reads and so has nothing to overlap. Q04 therefore does not strengthen the ASYNCHRONY argument; it strengthens IMP-002 (do not miss in the first place). Recorded explicitly so the Q04 relation is not misread as evidence for asynchrony.
Raw: Q04-cubrid-headline-telemetry-run2.json, profile-cubrid-callgraph.txt, q4-trace-cubrid.out.
improvements.mechanism_cubrid: pgbuf_fix_release() (page_buffer.c:2211) looks the page up; on a miss it calls fileio_read() (page_buffer.c:8464), which performs one pread of exactly one 16 KiB page (file_io.c:3935) on the calling query thread and blocks until the kernel has copied it. There is no asynchronous submission anywhere in the data path - the only aio_read in the tree is inside a pread() compatibility shim that immediately calls aio_suspend (file_io.c:3745-3767) - and no per-scan readahead hint, the single posix_fadvise being a mount-time whole-volume advise (file_io.c:3050). The multi-page primitive fileio_read_pages() (file_io.c:4211) exists but is wired only to the log paths. Consequently the page-cache copy and lookup cost appears as kernel time inside cub_server's query threads: at matched plan shape rep_movs_alternative 5.95%; in the native index-nested-loop plan rep_movs_alternative 13.83% plus filemap_get_read_batch 1.82%, filemap_read 0.98%, xas_load 0.74% and xas_descend 0.70%.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: A sequential scan pulls buffers from a ReadStream (read_stream.c:1030), which looks ahead over the scan's block sequence and submits I/O through io_method=worker, so a separate io worker process (method_worker.c:482/687) performs the wait and the copy while the executor keeps processing buffers that are already available. Q03 measures 2.72 core-seconds of io worker CPU classified as auxiliary against only 0.78 core-seconds of kernel I/O inside the executor itself (next_uptodate_folio 2.48% + rep_movs_alternative 1.58% of 19.28 executor core-seconds). BAS_BULKREAD (freelist.c:442) separately confines a large scan to a small ring so it does not evict the rest of the pool - that effect belongs to IMP-002, not here.

The synchronous nature shows up as 207,274 context switches in 20.002 s (2.734 K/s) against PostgreSQL's 7,880 (71/s), a 38.5x rate difference, and as 4.44% of CUBRID's profile in the page-cache read path (rep_movs_alternative 3.66% + filemap_get_read_batch 0.51% + filemap_read 0.27%). Q08 also reproduces the Q03/Q04/Q06 finding that cubrid statdump's global perfmon counters are frozen (delta 0 across a verified 4-statement block AND across a trivial serial count(*)), so all Q08 I/O evidence comes from /proc/<pid>/io.
improvements.ranking_rationale: Ranked third of the three Q03 candidates. Below IMP-006 on measured share of the matched-shape CPU excess (7.9% versus 18.7%) and below it on generality, since this only bites when the working set exceeds the buffer pool - true for Q03 (13.06 GiB against an 8 GiB pool) but not for Q02 (1.86 GiB). Above IMP-005 on runtime effect, which IMP-005 does not have at all. It was initially ranked P1 alongside IMP-006 on a read-combining argument; that argument was withdrawn when the syscall measurement showed CUBRID already moves more bytes per read call than PostgreSQL (17.2 versus 15.4 KiB), leaving only the critical-path placement effect, which is smaller and bounded. Its first implementation step is nevertheless the cheapest of the three candidates and has direct upstream precedent. Q04 demotes this relative to IMP-002: with PostgreSQL at zero physical reads there is no cross-engine asynchrony contrast on Q04, and the same 1.160 core-s is fully addressable by retention, so the marginal value of asynchrony on this query is bounded by what IMP-002 leaves behind, not added to it.

alternative: IMP-002 (reduce the NUMBER of misses via replacement policy) rather than the cost per miss; effects are NOT summed
relations.note: Complementary to IMP-002 and disjoint from IMP-006 by profile symbol. IMP-002 attacks how many pages must be re-read, IMP-007 attacks where the cost of each re-read is paid. Effects are not summed: part of the 1.68x byte difference against PostgreSQL belongs to IMP-002's retention deficit, not to this candidate.

improvements.root_cause_title: Every data-page buffer miss is served by a synchronous single-page pread on the query thread itself, with no asynchronous submission and no per-scan readahead, so page-cache copy and lookup cost is paid inside the executor's critical path instead of being overlapped by separate I/O processes
improvements.upstream_precedent: Yes for the readahead step: a05cfaa59 [CBRD-22319] 'add system parameter for read ahead fadvise' (#1282) introduced exactly the posix_fadvise machinery this candidate would extend from mount-time to per-scan, and it is an ancestor of the pinned build. No precedent for batching data-page reads through fileio_read_pages() (log-only to date) and none for asynchronous data-page I/O.
improvements.validation_criteria: (1) At matched plan shape, the kernel band charged to cub_server query threads falls below 3% of profiled self cost with unchanged bytes read, and controlled-plan median wall drops below 6.5 s with byte-identical output versus sink/Q03-cubrid-hash-block.out; (2) native Q03 median wall no worse than 4.808 s; (3) total_query_cpu does not increase - explicitly guarding against trading critical-path CPU for a larger total, which is the failure mode PostgreSQL's 0.432 core-seconds per GiB illustrates; (4) /proc syscr per statement recorded before and after so any submission-count claim is measured rather than assumed; (5) no change to any Q01-Q22 result; (6) double-write-buffer and page-validation paths exercised by the existing recovery tests.

improvements.correctness_risk: Medium. Comparison semantics - coercion rules, NULL handling, total versus ordinal order, collation for string domains - must be preserved exactly, and a wrongly cached domain decision silently changes predicate results rather than crashing. The constant-pre-coercion sub-step is materially lower risk because it changes WHEN a coercion happens, not WHICH one.

improvements.implementation_direction: Specialize the sarg path at plan time instead of per row. eval_fnc() (query_evaluator.c:2590) already resolves a single-node type; extend that from choosing an evaluator FUNCTION to binding a resolved comparison for the concrete (domain, domain, REL_OP) triple, so eval_value_rel_cmp()'s per-call tp_domain_resolve_default()/tp_value_coerce() prologue at :178-262 runs once per scan rather than once per row. Cheapest first step: the constant side of a range sarg is known at compile time, so pre-coerce it to the column domain when the predicate is built and take the fast path unconditionally thereafter.

improvements.priority_justification: Raised from P1 to P0 on Q06 evidence. On Q04 this band was 0.825 core-s and 18.1% of that query's CPU excess, which justified P1. On Q06 - a bare three-sarg full scan with F_plan = 1.0000 and F_work = 1.0000, i.e. no plan or cardinality confound whatsoever - the same root cause accounts for 7.624 core-s and 54.4% of a 14.023 core-s CPU excess, and 4.23x on the directly comparable predicate band. Parallelizing a subquery body changes nothing semantically for a read-only uncorrelated block, but the body must be proved parallel-safe by the existing px_scan_checker rules (it already walks dptr_list/scan_ptr chains), and the trace-merge path for nested chains is known to be fragile - IMP-005 documents a (k-1)x counter multiplication that appears exactly when a scan_ptr chain is merged under parallel workers. Raising this subquery's degree above 1 would put Q05's 5-level scan_ptr chain onto that path for the first time, so IMP-005 must be fixed first or validated together.

improvements.effect_range: Direct A/B: removing the amplification takes CUBRID from 458,209 to 158,930 physical page reads per statement, i.e. -4.57 GiB of page-cache traffic. If the kernel read band scales with bytes, the 2.543 core-s band falls to about 0.882 core-s, releasing roughly 1.66 core-s of the 14.023 core-s Q06 CPU excess (11.8%). That is also 66% of CUBRID's measured 2.500 core-s parallel CPU inflation (20.629 core-s serial -> 23.128 core-s at 6 units), which is the independent upper bound. No wall claim is made beyond that: at 5.97 active units a CPU saving converts to wall only in proportion to utilization, so the expected wall gain is about 0.28 s of 3.875 s. On a host where the data did NOT fit the OS page cache the same 4.57 GiB would be device I/O and the effect would be far larger; this campaign's host makes Q06 the CHEAP case, not the expensive one.
improvements.evidence_event: physical page reads per statement for one full scan of the same relation in the same pool, as a function of nothing but the number of scan units. Denominator: lineitem = 682,937 CUBRID heap pages of 16 KiB in a 524,288-page (8 GiB) pool, so the arithmetically unavoidable overflow is 682,937 - 524,288 = 158,649 pages per statement. Measured by /proc/<cub_server>/io syscr deltas divided by the statement count, cross-checked against the trace's own ioread counter.
improvements.explanation: One scan thread reads 158,930 pages per statement - the predicted overflow to within 0.18% - so CUBRID's replacement policy retains the entire pool's worth of the relation and behaves optimally. The identical scan on 3, 6 or 12 pooled workers reads 468,980 / 458,209 / 459,242 pages, retaining only 213,957-224,728, and the degradation is flat in DOP rather than proportional to it: it is a step change caused by WHICH LRU list receives the pages, not by concurrency pressure. PostgreSQL, whose scan-resistance is a per-scan strategy ring rather than a per-thread list, reads 76,987 pages serially and 78,482 at DOP 5 against a predicted overflow of 76,552 - a 1.9% DOP effect against CUBRID's 188%.
improvements.implementation_direction: Propagate the parent's LRU identity into the parallel-scan worker's thread entry at src/query/parallel/px_scan/px_scan_task.cpp:94, next to the existing m_px_orig_thread_entry assignment: copy m_parent_thread_p->private_lru_index and call pgbuf_thread_variables_init() so m_is_private_lru_enabled follows, and clear both again on retire (thread_entry_task.cpp:75-76 already does). All N workers of one scan then share the ONE private list of the session that owns the query, which is the same list the serial path uses, so the serial retention behaviour is reproduced exactly rather than approximated. Cheaper and less invasive alternative if sharing one private list across workers proves contended: keep the shared list but insert scan pages at the TOP rather than the MIDDLE when the fixing thread is a parallel-scan worker of a sequential scan; that recovers most of the retention without touching thread identity. The structurally cleanest fix - and the one PostgreSQL's design argues for - is to make scan-resistance a property of the SCAN (a per-scan ring/strategy handed to pgbuf_fix, as in freelist.c:426) instead of a property of the fixing thread, which removes the whole class of defect rather than this instance.

measurement.pool_state_dependence: The parallel read count is itself unstable across pool states while the serial one is not: the three headline-regime telemetry blocks all measured 608,510 reads per statement (rchar 39,874,595,032-096 bytes per 4-statement block, i.e. 89.1% miss) while the lru_ab probe, which drives each variant to its own equilibrium with two extra passes first, measured 458,209-468,980 across DOP 3/6/12 (67.1-68.7%). Serial measured 158,930 and 162,257 in the same two settings (23.27% and 23.76%). Read amplification is therefore 2.88x-3.83x depending on pool state, and the section 12 headline regime sits at the 3.83x end. That the PARALLEL figure wobbles by 33% while the SERIAL figure is pinned to the arithmetic overflow is additional evidence that the parallel path's retention is unstable, not merely lower.

improvements.root_cause_title: A heap scan's newly read pages are inserted at the TOP of the session's private LRU list when the scan runs on the client transaction thread, but only into the MIDDLE of a round-robin SHARED LRU list when the same scan runs on pooled parallel-query workers, because a worker's thread entry is recycled with private_lru_index = -1 and the parallel-scan task never propagates its parent's LRU identity - so going parallel silently discards the buffer pool's scan-resistance and re-reads 2.88x the pages
improvements.upstream_precedent: No prior CBRD issue or PR that propagates the session's private LRU index into parallel-scan workers was identified in the pinned tree at 607f1ee9. The pattern of propagating per-session executor state into px workers IS established at px_scan_task.cpp:94 for m_px_orig_thread_entry, so this is an extension of an accepted pattern rather than a new one. On the PostgreSQL side the corresponding change is ancient and settled - BAS_BULKREAD ring buffers for large scans - which is why PostgreSQL's numbers here are DOP-independent; that is a precedent for the design, not for the CUBRID patch.
improvements.validation_criteria: (1) Q01-Q22 results byte-identical - mandatory for any buffer change even though placement cannot affect correctness. (2) Q06 CUBRID physical reads per statement fall from 458,209 to within 5% of the serial 158,930 at DOP 6, measured the same way (/proc/<cub_server>/io syscr delta / statement count) and cross-checked against the trace ioread counter. (3) The measured value stays within 5% of 158,930 at DOP 3 and DOP 12 as well, since DOP independence is the property being restored. (4) The rep_movs_alternative + filemap_* kernel band falls from 11.01% to under 5% of profiled self cost. (5) Q06 CUBRID median wall improves against 3.875 s under the same warm_establish + measure_block protocol with the WARM gate still CONVERGED, and the block-to-block spread does not exceed the 3.08% recorded here. (6) No regression in Q01/Q03/Q04 physical reads - those queries' IMP-002 evidence must be RE-MEASURED with this fix, because Q06 shows their 'pool cannot retain a marginally oversized working set' conclusion may in fact be this defect. (7) A high-DOP contention check: cub_server mutex/latch time on the private list must not rise above its current 3.50% buffer-manager band.

improvements.explanation: CUBRID derives its parallel degree from the driving relation's page count and then leaves its coordinator idle, so a plan whose per-page work is three orders of magnitude above a bare scan gets 5 executing threads out of a configured 6; PostgreSQL gets 5 workers plus a participating leader on the identical shape, and prices the leader in its cost model.
improvements.implementation_direction: Two independently shippable steps. (a) Let the coordinator execute a task: in manager::next(), when the merged-list read would block and an unclaimed input range remains, run one task inline on the calling thread - the input handler already partitions by range, so no new partitioning is needed, and this is the direct analogue of PostgreSQL's need_to_scan_locally. (b) Make the SCAN auto_degree aware of the per-page work of the scan_ptr chain hanging off the spec rather than of the driving relation's page count alone, and reach the configured parallelism when that work justifies it; the cheapest correct version multiplies num_pages by the estimated inner-probe count already available in the plan the spec came from, keeping plan_generation.c:3204-3234 consistent.

Remainder 1.1476x = the longer CUBRID serial tail (0.337 s vs 0.232 s) plus a 7.5% straggler spread across the five CUBRID workers (heap time 1018..1094 ms).
improvements.mechanism_cubrid: For a parallel heap scan CUBRID calls compute_parallel_degree(SCAN, num_pages, hint). The SCAN branch computes auto_degree = floor(log2(num_pages / parallel_scan_page_threshold)) + 2 then degree = MIN(auto_degree, parallelism). Q08's driving relation part has 24,353 heap pages and parallel_scan_page_threshold defaults to 2048 (a PRM_HIDDEN parameter), so x = 11, floor(log2 11) = 3, auto_degree = 5 and MIN(5, 6) = 5: the configured parallelism=6 is never reached. The degree is a function of the DRIVING relation's page count alone - it cannot see that each of those pages drives about 16 lineitem index probes plus an orders and a customer PK probe, i.e. that per-page work here is three orders of magnitude above a bare scan. Then manager::start_tasks() pushes exactly m_parallelism tasks to the worker pool and returns; the calling transaction thread's only scan-related work in manager::next() is m_result_handler->read() on the merged list. Active units therefore equal the degree: the coordinator contributes 0.20 core-s of the 4.34 core-s statement and never executes a scan task.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: compute_parallel_worker() also derives workers from a page-count logarithm (log3 ladder on min_parallel_table_scan_size / min_parallel_index_scan_size) but on the same relation returns the full max_parallel_workers_per_gather cap of 5, and then the leader ALSO executes the plan: nodeGatherMerge.c:253-254 'if (parallel_leader_participation || node->nreaders == 0)' and :403-404 'Slot 0 is always for the leader. Leader always calls ExecProcNode()', with nodeGather.c:214-215 doing the same for plain Gather. The cost model knows it - get_parallel_divisor() adds 1.0 - 0.3 * nworkers of leader contribution to the divisor. Measured result: loops=6 on every node under the Gather Merge and peak 6.2449 active units.

improvements.explanation: CUBRID's LRU replacement policy needs list order, so it pays a mutex-protected unlink/relink plus zone rebalance on every unfix of a resident page; PostgreSQL's clock sweep needs no order, so it pays one atomic counter bump - which is why CUBRID's 6.6x smaller tuple-touch count only converts into a 16% CPU advantage instead of a wall win.
improvements.implementation_direction: Three options, cheapest first. (a) Extend the existing age-based suppression: pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb's own comment already documents 'if a page is quickly fixed several times, its age is really small ... we don't boost it', implemented in pgbuf_unlatch_bcb_upon_unfix; a random index-probe workload is the opposite case - a cold SINGLE touch of a zone-2/3 page - which that rule does not cover. Suppress the boost when the BCB's hit count since insertion is 1 and the fix was a read-only visibility fetch. (b) Batch the boost: record boost intent in the BCB and apply it under one mutex acquisition per N unfixes. (c) Replace the LRU lists with a clock sweep over the BCB array, removing the list and the per-list mutex entirely; freelist.c StrategyGetBuffer() is the reference shape.

CUBRID retires 0.7391x PostgreSQL's instructions (252.359 G vs 341.463 G) at 1.0909x the IPC (1.20 vs 1.10), and switches context 38.5x more often (2.734 K/s vs 71/s).
improvements.mechanism_cubrid: pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb() is called on unfix of any BCB that lives in LRU zone 2 or 3. It takes pthread_mutex_lock(&lru_list->mutex), calls pgbuf_remove_from_lru_list() to unlink the BCB from its current position, pgbuf_lru_add_bcb_to_top() to relink it at the head, and then pgbuf_lru_adjust_zone1() or pgbuf_lru_adjust_zones(), which walk the list to re-balance zone boundaries through pgbuf_bcb_change_zone(). On Q08's dominant path this runs once PER HEAP ROW: heap_get_visible_version() -> heap_clean_get_context -> pgbuf_unfix -> pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb, verified in the call graph at 5.38% of the parallel-query threads' cost. Q08 performs about 1.35 M fix/unfix pairs per statement (403,487 lineitem + 403,487 orders + 122,404 customer + 24,254 supplier heap lookups, each preceded by its index descent), so the list is reordered under a mutex about a million times per statement on pages that were already resident.
improvements.mechanism_postgresql: UnpinBuffer() / UnpinBufferNoOwner() decrement a PROCESS-LOCAL PrivateRefCountEntry->refcount and, only when it reaches zero, issue one pg_atomic_fetch_sub_u64(&buf->state, BUF_REFCOUNT_ONE). PinBuffer() bumps usagecount INSIDE the same compare-and-swap that takes the pin ('Default case: increase usagecount unless already max'). PostgreSQL's replacement algorithm is a clock sweep over the buffer array, so there is no ordered list to maintain, no per-list mutex to acquire and no zone rebalance to run. Searched src/storage/page_buffer.c for clock / sweep / usage_count / usagecount: CUBRID has no clock-sweep equivalent - the file implements private and shared LRU lists with zones 1/2/3.

improvements.risk: medium-high on performance regression: suppressing or batching boosts changes eviction order, so a workload whose hot set currently survives BECAUSE of aggressive boosting could start missing - and Q08 measures that a miss costs 0.4099 core-s per GiB of re-read. Option (a) is the only variant shippable without a full buffer-pool re-validation.
improvements.root_cause_title: Every page unfix on a HIT path performs mutex-protected LRU doubly-linked-list surgery plus zone rebalancing (pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb), so a plan that touches 6.6x fewer tuples than PostgreSQL's nets only a 16% total-CPU advantage: 27.41% of CUBRID's profile sits in pgbuf fix/unfix/LRU and 5.32% in libpthread, against PostgreSQL's 3.70% clock-sweep pin/unpin with no list and no mutex
improvements.upstream_precedent: No precedent in the pinned CUBRID history for removing or batching the LRU boost. The closest thing is the age-based suppression rule the same function's comment documents at page_buffer.c:10086-10098, which shows the cost was anticipated by the original author for a repeat-fix pattern - and is why option (a) is proposed first.
improvements.validation_criteria: pgbuf_lru_boost_bcb plus libpthread share on Q08 drops below 3% with pgbuf_fix_release unchanged; Q08 total_query_cpu drops by >= 0.3 core-s per statement; Q08 per-statement read-syscall count does NOT increase (the regression that matters - a worse eviction order shows up as more pool churn, which Q08 measures at 0.4099 core-s per GiB); Q01, Q03, Q04 and Q06 walls not regressed, since those are the sequential-scan queries whose retention IMP-002 already flags.
